To tutor someone means to teach a person privately, giving them focused, one-on-one (or very small group) attention in a specific subject.

Think of it this way: a regular school teacher stands in front of 30 students and teaches everyone at the same time. But when someone tutors you, they sit down with just you — and everything they say, every example they give, every question they answer, is directed entirely at you and your needs. That personal, close, dedicated teaching is what the verb "to tutor" captures.

When you say someone tutors, it tells you three things at once:

  1. There is a teacher (the one doing the tutoring)
  2. There is a learner (the one being tutored)
  3. The teaching is personal and focused — not delivered to a crowd

For example:

  • "She tutors him in mathematics." → She privately teaches him math.
  • "He tutors students every weekend." → He gives private lessons to students on weekends.
  • "She was tutored in English before her exams." → Someone privately coached her in English to prepare for her tests.

The single most important thing about the verb "to tutor" is the idea of private, personalized instruction. This is what separates it from simply "to teach."

A teacher teaches. A tutor also teaches — but in a deeply personal way, adjusting every explanation to fit that one learner's pace, confusion, and gaps. When someone tutors you, they are not rushing ahead because 25 other students are waiting. They stay with you until you understand.

Almost anyone with greater knowledge in a subject can tutor someone who knows less. It is not limited to professional teachers. For example:

  • A university student can tutor a high school student in chemistry.
  • A retired professor can tutor an adult learner in history.
  • An older sibling can tutor a younger one in reading.
  • A professional language speaker can tutor someone in French or Spanish.

The word does not require that the tutor be a certified teacher. It only requires that one person is guiding another through learning, privately and directly.

People are tutored for two main reasons:

  1. To catch up — A student is falling behind in a subject and needs extra help beyond what the classroom provides. For example, a student who is struggling with algebra might be tutored to fill in the gaps in their understanding.
  2. To go further — A student is already doing well but wants to go deeper or faster than the classroom allows. For example, a gifted student might be tutored in advanced physics to prepare for a competition.

Both situations are perfectly natural uses of the word.

To tutor is a regular verb. Here is how it works in sentences:

  • Active: She tutors him in biology every Tuesday.

(She is the one giving the lessons; he is the one receiving them.)

  • Passive: He was tutored in biology by a medical student.

(He received private lessons; a medical student gave them.)

  • Without naming the subject: She tutors on weekends.

(She gives private lessons — the subject doesn't need to be stated here.)

  • Without naming the student: He used to tutor at the local library.

(He used to give private lessons at the library — the specific student isn't mentioned.)

Notice that you can "tutor someone in a subject" — the preposition in is the natural companion when you name the subject being taught.
How It Differs From Similar Words

These words are close in meaning but not identical:

  • To teach — The broadest word. You can teach a class of hundreds. "Tutor" always implies something smaller and more personal.
  • To coach — Usually about improving performance or skill (sports, public speaking, confidence). "Tutor" leans more toward academic or intellectual subjects.
  • To train — Usually about building a practical skill through repeated practice (training someone to use a machine, to run faster). "Tutor" is more about understanding and knowledge.
  • To mentor — A mentor guides someone over a long period of time, often about life, career, or personal growth — much broader than one subject. "Tutor" is focused and specific.
  • To instruct — More formal, more procedural (you instruct someone to follow steps). "Tutor" is warmer and more flexible — it adjusts to the learner.

To tutor is to privately and personally teach someone, giving them your full, undivided attention, usually in a specific subject, and adjusting your teaching to fit exactly what that one person needs. It is teaching at its most human and most direct — not a lecture delivered to a crowd, but a conversation tailored to a single learner.

That is the full meaning of the word, with nothing left out.
